advances: Every strict counterexample to the locked polygonal problem gives arbitrarily close compatible smooth triples with positive boundary curvature, the same strict global depth failure, and the strict residual area inequalities. Consequently it suffices to exclude this auxiliary smooth counterexample class. At its attained middle optimum, three actual concurrent minimizing cuts obey full-chord first-moment identities and the central-chord inequality, with zero first variation at point tangencies. When the common outer chord length is positive, the two-parameter Hessian condition holds with the actual tangent slopes at the six chord endpoints. No supporting-edge subsegment is selected, and no transversality or positive-length assertion is made for the remaining cuts.
author: r132-smooth-reduction
proof:
First consider any compatible triple of compact two-dimensional convex bodies. A closed halfspace containing a specified point can be moved parallel to itself until its boundary passes through that point, producing a contained halfspace. Thus, for \(j\in\{0,1,2\}\), its exact depth at \((j,w)\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
h_S((j,w))=\min\Bigg\{&
\inf_{\substack{q\in\mathbb S^1\\\lambda\in\mathbb R}}
\sum_{i=0}^2
\left|A_i\cap\{x:q\cdot(x-w)+\lambda(i-j)\le0\}\right|,\\
&\sum_{i\le j}a_i,\quad \sum_{i\ge j}a_i
\Bigg\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
Indeed, any nonhorizontal normal has a nonzero planar component, which can be normalized to \(q\), leaving a real height slope \(\lambda\). The other two normals give the two displayed horizontal masses. In particular, their whole-slice boundary masses have not been replaced by a limiting tilted cut. Formula (11) is the boundary-through-point normalization of accepted fact \(949ce2fdf2e1e240\), now obtained directly without a polygonal assumption.

On a fixed compact neighborhood of a bounded set of points \(w\), choose \(B\) greater than every \(\|x-w\|\) with \(x\in\bigcup_i A_i\). For \(\lambda\ge B\), the sign of every summand with \(i\ne j\) is determined by \(i-j\), so its cap is exactly full or empty; the \(i=j\) cap is independent of \(\lambda\). The same holds for \(\lambda\le-B\). Therefore the infimum in (11) is a minimum over the fixed compact set \(\mathbb S^1\times[-B,B]\). The cap sum is jointly continuous in \(w,q,\lambda\): convergent parameters give convergent indicators except on a limiting affine line in each slice, and such a line has planar area zero. Dominated convergence applies. Uniform continuity on compact sets then shows that this minimum, and hence depth on each fixed height plane, is continuous. Its restriction to each compact \(A_j\) attains a maximum. This proves attainment in (1), and a polygonal counterexample has the positive uniform gap
\[
\gamma:=t-\mathcal D(A_0,A_1,A_2)>0.
\tag{12}
\]

We next establish the uniform comparison in (2). Extend \(h_\mu(y)=\inf_{H\ni y}\mu(H)\) to every point of the fixed set
\(\mathcal P=(\{0,1,2\}\times\mathbb R^2)\). For two triples, with measures \(\mu,\widetilde\mu\), put \(E=\sum_i|A_i\mathbin{\triangle}\widetilde A_i|\). Their signed difference has total variation \(E\): on each of the three disjoint planes its density is the difference of the two indicator functions. In particular,
\[
|\mu(H)-\widetilde\mu(H)|\le E
\quad\text{for every closed halfspace }H,
\qquad
|h_\mu(y)-h_{\widetilde\mu}(y)|\le E
\quad\text{for every }y.
\tag{13}
\]
The second inequality follows by taking infima over the same family \(\{H:y\in H\}\) in both directions.

Compatibility implies
\[
\operatorname{conv}(S)\cap\mathcal P=S.
\tag{14}
\]
At height zero or two, a convex combination with that height uses only that endpoint slice. At height one, group a convex combination by heights, with weights \(\theta_i\). Its height equation gives \(\theta_0=\theta_2\). The equal outer weights combine into a point of \((A_0+A_2)/2\), and the rest is a point of \(A_1\), so their combination belongs to \(A_1\). This also covers zero weights. Conversely all of \(S\) belongs to its convex hull.

If \(y\notin\operatorname{conv}(S)\), strict separation from this compact convex set gives a closed halfspace containing \(y\) and disjoint from \(S\), so \(h_\mu(y)=0\). Hence (14) yields
\[
\sup_{y\in\mathcal P}h_\mu(y)
=\max_{y\in S}h_\mu(y)
=\mathcal D(A_0,A_1,A_2).
\tag{15}
\]
Taking suprema in (13) over this same fixed \(\mathcal P\) proves the global depth comparison in (2). This argument includes moving maximizers and every horizontal or tilted cut. The estimate for total area follows from \(\big||A_i|-|\widetilde A_i|\big|\le|A_i\mathbin{\triangle}\widetilde A_i|\).

We now construct the smooth bodies from the original polygons. Let \(B_2\) denote the closed unit disk, let \(u(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\), and let \(p(\theta)=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)\). The original support functions are
\[
h_i(\theta)=\max_{x\in A_i}u(\theta)\cdot x.
\]
They are continuous and \(2\pi\)-periodic. The support function of a Minkowski sum is the sum of support functions, since the two maxima are independent. Thus compatibility gives \(h_0+h_2\le2h_1\) at every angle.

Choose the same positive smooth periodic kernel for all three slices:
\[
\varphi_\varepsilon(\theta)
=\frac{\exp((\cos\theta-1)/\varepsilon)}
 {\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\exp((\cos v-1)/\varepsilon)\,dv},
\qquad
h_i^\varepsilon(\theta)
=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\varphi_\varepsilon(v)h_i(\theta-v)\,dv+\varepsilon.
\tag{16}
\]
The kernel has integral one. For \(0<\delta<\pi\), its mass on \(\delta\le|v|\le\pi\) is at most
\[
\frac{2\pi}{\delta}
\exp\left(\frac{\cos\delta-\cos(\delta/2)}{\varepsilon}\right),
\]
because its denominator is at least
\(\delta\exp((\cos(\delta/2)-1)/\varepsilon)\). This bound tends to zero. Uniform continuity of each \(h_i\) therefore proves
\[
\delta_\varepsilon:=
\max_i\|h_i^\varepsilon-h_i\|_\infty\longrightarrow0.
\tag{17}
\]
Differentiating the smooth kernel proves that every \(h_i^\varepsilon\) is \(C^\infty\). Positivity and the use of the same kernel and same added disk support give exactly
\[
h_0^\varepsilon+h_2^\varepsilon\le2h_1^\varepsilon.
\tag{18}
\]

We verify directly that the functions in (16) define the asserted bodies. On an angular interval where a polygon vertex \(v\) is exposed, its support function is \(v\cdot u(\theta)\), so \(h''+h=0\) there. At the outward normal angle \(\theta_k\) of an edge of length \(L_k\), the exposed vertex changes in the direction \(p(\theta_k)\) by \(L_kp(\theta_k)\). Thus the one-sided derivative of \(h\) has upward jump \(L_k\). Integration by parts on the finitely many intervening intervals shows that \(h''+h\), as a distribution on the circle, is \(\sum_kL_k\delta_{\theta_k}\). Convolving this identity in (16) gives
\[
h_i^\varepsilon(\theta)+(h_i^\varepsilon)''(\theta)
=\sum_kL_{ik}\varphi_\varepsilon(\theta-\theta_{ik})+\varepsilon
>0.
\tag{19}
\]

Here is a direct support-function construction for any smooth periodic \(g\) with \(g+g''>0\). Define
\[
x_g(\theta)=g(\theta)u(\theta)+g'(\theta)p(\theta),
\qquad
x_g'(\theta)=(g(\theta)+g''(\theta))p(\theta).
\tag{20}
\]
For a fixed angle \(\alpha\),
\[
\frac{d}{d\theta}\bigl(u(\alpha)\cdot x_g(\theta)\bigr)
=(g(\theta)+g''(\theta))\sin(\alpha-\theta).
\tag{21}
\]
On one period starting at \(\alpha\), this expression is strictly negative on the first open semicircle and strictly positive on the second. Hence the unique maximizing point of this projection is \(x_g(\alpha)\), and its value is \(g(\alpha)\).

Let \(K_g\) be the convex hull of the curve in (20). It is compact and has support function \(g\) by (21). It has nonempty interior: otherwise its curve would lie in a line, whereas its nonzero tangent vectors in (20) take every direction. Each supporting face of \(K_g\) is the singleton \(x_g(\alpha)\), again by the uniqueness in (21). Every boundary point of a full-dimensional compact convex set has a supporting line, so the boundary of \(K_g\) is exactly this curve. Formula (21) also shows that \(x_g(\alpha)=x_g(\theta)\) forces \(\alpha=\theta\) modulo \(2\pi\). Thus this is a regular simple closed \(C^\infty\) boundary, all its support faces are points, and the body is strictly convex. Its curvature is positive, with value \(1/(g+g'')\): differentiating (20) once more gives
\(\det(x_g',x_g'')=(g+g'')^2\) and \(\|x_g'\|=g+g''\).
This constructs and verifies the smooth body without assuming an unchecked support-function regularity theorem.

Apply this construction to \(g=h_i^\varepsilon\), defining \(A_i^\varepsilon=K_{h_i^\varepsilon}\). A compact convex set is the intersection of its supporting halfplanes, by separation. Consequently (18) implies \((A_0^\varepsilon+A_2^\varepsilon)/2\subseteq A_1^\varepsilon\).

Support-function order and separation also show from (17) that
\[
A_i^\varepsilon\subseteq A_i+\delta_\varepsilon B_2,
\qquad A_i\subseteq A_i^\varepsilon+\delta_\varepsilon B_2,
\]
so the Hausdorff distances tend to zero. For an explicit area comparison, fix \(v_i+\eta_iB_2\subseteq A_i\), where \(\eta_i>0\). If \(\delta_\varepsilon<\eta_i\), define the two homothetic bodies
\[
A_i^-=
v_i+\left(1-\frac{\delta_\varepsilon}{\eta_i}\right)(A_i-v_i),
\qquad
A_i^+=
v_i+\left(1+\frac{\delta_\varepsilon}{\eta_i}\right)(A_i-v_i).
\]
The inequality \(h_i(\theta)-u(\theta)\cdot v_i\ge\eta_i\) and (17) imply that the support of \(A_i^-\) is at most \(h_i^\varepsilon\), while the support of \(A_i^+\) is at least \(h_i^\varepsilon\). Both \(A_i\) and \(A_i^\varepsilon\) therefore lie between \(A_i^-\) and \(A_i^+\). Taking the area of the intervening region gives
\[
|A_i^\varepsilon\mathbin{\triangle}A_i|
\le |A_i^+|-|A_i^-|
=\frac{4a_i\delta_\varepsilon}{\eta_i}\longrightarrow0.
\tag{22}
\]
This proves all convergence and comparison assertions in (2). Equations (2) and (12) give the quantitative persistence estimate
\[
\frac{2T^\varepsilon}{9}
-\mathcal D(A_0^\varepsilon,A_1^\varepsilon,A_2^\varepsilon)
\ge\gamma-\frac{11}{9}E_\varepsilon.
\tag{23}
\]
Choose \(E_\varepsilon<9\gamma/22\) to retain a gap greater than \(\gamma/2\).

The original polygonal counterexample satisfies the strict area strip of accepted fact \(15bb2c1680a0254e\), and \(r<3/8\) by accepted fact \(291c24bb45bd4946\). Area convergence implies convergence of \(M,m,r,s\), since the areas stay positive and maximum and minimum are continuous. Each positive difference in (4) is a continuous function of the positive areas; the same is true if the maximum and minimum in (4) are expanded into their separate inequalities. Taking \(\varepsilon\) sufficiently small retains at least half every original positive difference. This proves the area-margin assertion. The weak area compatibility inequality needs no separate perturbation argument; compatibility of the actual bodies has already been proved. In fact the strict lower inequalities displayed in (4) also dominate that weak area lower bound, as in accepted fact \(15bb2c1680a0254e\).

We now use \(A_i\) for an arbitrary smooth auxiliary triple as specified after (4). Formula (11) and its compactness argument remain valid. Middle depth is zero on \(\partial A_1\). To prove this, take a supporting unit normal \(n\) at \(w\in\partial A_1\), and put \(b=n\cdot w=\max_{A_1}n\cdot x\). If \(h_i(n)=\max_{A_i}n\cdot x\), compatibility gives \(h_0(n)+h_2(n)\le2b\). Choose
\[
\lambda\in[h_0(n)-b,\,b-h_2(n)].
\]
The halfspace \(\{(h,x):n\cdot(x-w)+\lambda(h-1)\ge0\}\) meets each body only in a supporting line or the empty set, and hence has mass zero. At an interior middle point, a disk centered there and contained in \(A_1\) contributes a fixed positive semidisk area to every nonhorizontal boundary-through-point halfspace; both horizontal masses are also positive. Middle depth is therefore positive at every such point. Its maximum is attained at some \(z\in\operatorname{int}A_1\), with \(0<d<t\).

Since \(a_i<T/2\), the two horizontal middle masses are \(T-a_2,T-a_0>T/2>t\). Let
\[
G(w,q,\lambda)=
\sum_{i=0}^2
\left|A_i\cap\{x:q\cdot(x-w)+\lambda(i-1)\le0\}\right|.
\]
On a compact neighborhood of \(A_1\), use the compact parameter set \(\mathbb S^1\times[-B,B]\) from (11). The active set
\(\mathcal A=\{(q,\lambda):G(z,q,\lambda)=d\}\)
is nonempty and compact.

The convex hull of its planar unit normals contains zero. Otherwise strict separation supplies \(v\in\mathbb R^2\) and \(c>0\) such that \(q\cdot v>2c\) for every active normal. The compact set of parameters with \(q\cdot v\le c\), if nonempty, has a positive gap above \(d\); uniform continuity preserves this gap when \(z\) is replaced by \(z+uv\) for sufficiently small \(u>0\). For the remaining parameters, all three cap thresholds increase by \(u q\cdot v>uc\). Their middle caps increase by at least a fixed positive multiple of \(u\), uniformly in the direction: a fixed disk centered at \(z\) inside \(A_1\) has uniformly positive chord length in all strips of sufficiently small width through its center. The outer cap areas cannot decrease. The horizontal terms already exceed \(d\). Thus every cut has mass uniformly greater than \(d\) at \(z+uv\), contradicting maximality. This proves the convex-hull assertion.

The planar convex-hull theorem selects at most three active normals with zero in their convex hull. One unit normal cannot suffice. If two suffice they are opposite. For opposite active normals \(q,-q\), with slopes \(\lambda,\lambda'\), their middle halfplanes cover the whole plane. Their height-zero halfplanes cover the plane when \(\lambda+\lambda'\ge0\), and their height-two halfplanes cover it when \(\lambda+\lambda'\le0\). Hence their two masses have sum at least \(a_1+m\), giving \(2d\ge a_1+m\). But \(M<T/2\) implies \(M<a_1+m\), so
\[
2d<2t=\frac{4T}{9}
<\frac{8(a_1+m)}9<a_1+m,
\]
a contradiction. A minimal selected family therefore contains exactly three normals, with positive convex coefficients. Equal normals would be redundant, and opposite ones have been excluded, so the three unit normals are pairwise nonparallel. This proves (5).

We derive the first variations directly for these smooth bodies. Fix one active cut and omit its index \(j\). Put \(L_i=A_i\cap\{x:q\cdot(x-z)+\lambda(i-1)=0\}\). For arbitrary \(u\in\mathbb R^2\) and \(\tau\in\mathbb R\), vary the cut to
\[
(q+\eta u)\cdot(x-z)+(\lambda+\eta\tau)(i-1)\le0.
\tag{24}
\]
For sufficiently small \(|\eta|\), its planar normal is nonzero; dividing the normal and slope by its norm gives an admissible unit-normal cut through \((1,z)\). Thus the total mass in (24) has a local minimum at \(\eta=0\).

Choose a unit \(p\perp q\), set \(\xi=q\cdot(x-z)\) and \(\upsilon=p\cdot(x-z)\), and write \(u=u_nq+u_tp\). At slice \(i\), the cutoff in the \(\xi\) coordinate is
\[
\xi\le
\frac{-\lambda(i-1)-\eta(u_t\upsilon+\tau(i-1))}
 {1+\eta u_n}.
\tag{25}
\]
Its derivative at zero is
\(-[u_n\xi_i+u_t\upsilon+\tau(i-1)]\), where \(\xi_i=-\lambda(i-1)\). For a fixed \(\upsilon\), the intersection of \(A_i\) with that coordinate line is an interval, possibly empty or a singleton, and its truncated length is a 1-Lipschitz function of the cutoff. Except at the at most two \(\upsilon\)-coordinates of boundary points in \(L_i\), this truncated length is differentiable at the initial cutoff: its derivative is the cutoff derivative when the initial point is in the interval interior, and is zero outside the interval. The exceptional set has one point at a tangent cut and is empty if the boundary line misses the body. The statement about at most two points uses strict convexity, so there is no positive supporting edge.

On the bounded range of \(\upsilon\) meeting \(A_i\), the difference quotients of (25) are uniformly bounded for small \(|\eta|\). Fubini and dominated convergence therefore give the two-sided derivative
\[
\left.\frac{d}{d\eta}
\left|A_i\cap\{x:(q+\eta u)\cdot(x-z)
                 +(\lambda+\eta\tau)(i-1)\le0\}\right|
\right|_{\eta=0}
=-\int_{L_i}
  \bigl[u\cdot(x-z)+\tau(i-1)\bigr]\,d\mathcal H_1(x).
\tag{26}
\]
At an empty or singleton section the integral is zero. In particular a tangent support section contributes zero first variation from both sides, even though its cap can appear or disappear under perturbation. This proves the required tangent assertion without assigning an artificial edge length.

Local minimality and the existence of the two-sided derivatives force the sum of (26) to vanish for every \(u,\tau\). Taking \(u=0\) gives \(-\mathcal H_1(L_0)+\mathcal H_1(L_2)=0\). Taking arbitrary \(u\) and \(\tau=0\) gives the vector first-moment equation in (6). The middle line passes through \(z\in\operatorname{int}A_1\), so \(b>0\). A positive section of a strictly convex body crosses its interior. At either endpoint it cannot be tangent to the smooth boundary, because the tangent line of a convex smooth boundary is supporting. Thus positive outer sections, when they occur, are full transverse chords.

When \(\ell>0\), compatibility puts the segment \((L_0+L_2)/2\) on the middle cut line and inside \(A_1\). It has length \(\ell\) and midpoint \(c=(c_0+c_2)/2\). Hence \(\ell\le b\) and \(\|c-c_1\|\le(b-\ell)/2\). The first moment is
\[
b(c_1-z)+2\ell(c-z)=0,
\]
which proves (7) and gives
\[
\|z-c_1\|
=\frac{2\ell}{b+2\ell}\|c-c_1\|
\le\frac{\ell(b-\ell)}{b+2\ell}.
\]
If \(\ell=0\), the same moment identity instead gives \(c_1=z\), so these bounds still hold without defining outer midpoints. Finally, on \(0\le x\le1\), the derivative of \(x(1-x)/(1+2x)\) is \((1-2x-2x^2)/(1+2x)^2\); its maximum is \(1-\sqrt3/2\), attained at \(x=(\sqrt3-1)/2\). Taking \(x=\ell/b\) proves all of (6). These are the smooth full-section counterparts of the selected-section conclusions of accepted fact \(e4a8e2c026dd7346\), now established from the actual derivatives.

It remains to prove (9). Fix a cut with \(\ell_j>0\), so all three sections are transverse. Near each endpoint, smoothness and transversality give a \(C^\infty\) graph
\[
\upsilon=f_{ij}^{\pm}(\xi),\qquad
f_{ij}^{\pm}(-\lambda_j(i-1))=\upsilon_{ij}^{\pm},\qquad
(f_{ij}^{\pm})'(-\lambda_j(i-1))=k_{ij}^{\pm}.
\]
For arbitrary real \(\beta,\tau\), vary the cut by
\[
(q_j+\eta\beta p_j)\cdot(w-z)
+(\lambda_j+\eta\tau)(h-1)\le0.
\tag{27}
\]
The normal can be divided by \(\sqrt{1+\eta^2\beta^2}\), together with the slope, without changing the halfspace. Thus no unit-normal correction is omitted.

The two moving endpoint coordinates satisfy
\[
\upsilon_{ij}^{\pm}(\eta)
=f_{ij}^{\pm}\!\left(
 -\lambda_j(i-1)
 -\eta\bigl(\beta\upsilon_{ij}^{\pm}(\eta)+\tau(i-1)\bigr)\right).
\tag{28}
\]
At \(\eta=0\), the derivative of this implicit equation with respect to its endpoint variable is one. The implicit function theorem gives smooth moving endpoints, jointly also for the two free cut parameters. Transversality is open, so these are the endpoints of the nearby full chord; convexity excludes any additional intersections. Differentiating (28) yields
\[
(\upsilon_{ij}^{\pm})'(0)
=-k_{ij}^{\pm}\bigl(\beta\upsilon_{ij}^{\pm}+\tau(i-1)\bigr).
\tag{29}
\]
If \(F_i(\eta)\) is the slice cap area in (27), Fubini with the moving cutoff
\(\xi=-\lambda_j(i-1)-\eta(\beta\upsilon+\tau(i-1))\)
gives, for every sufficiently small \(\eta\),
\[
F_i'(\eta)
=-\int_{\upsilon_{ij}^-(\eta)}^{\upsilon_{ij}^+(\eta)}
 \bigl(\beta\upsilon+\tau(i-1)\bigr)\,d\upsilon.
\tag{30}
\]
The endpoint smoothness just proved permits differentiation of this formula. Using (29),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left.\frac{d^2}{d\eta^2}\sum_iF_i(\eta)\right|_{\eta=0}
&=\sum_{i=0}^2\left[
 k_{ij}^+\bigl(\beta\upsilon_{ij}^++\tau(i-1)\bigr)^2
 -k_{ij}^-\bigl(\beta\upsilon_{ij}^-+\tau(i-1)\bigr)^2
 \right]\\
&=\Theta_j\beta^2+2\Gamma_j\beta\tau+\Delta_j\tau^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{31}
\]
Only the first derivatives of the endpoint graphs occur because the first area derivative is already the chord integral (30). Boundary curvature derivatives are not missing terms. The cut is genuinely minimizing through the fixed point, so this quadratic form is nonnegative for every \(\beta,\tau\). Positive semidefiniteness of its real symmetric two-by-two matrix is exactly (9), including the cases of a zero diagonal entry. This proves the claimed extension of the transverse Hessian formula of accepted fact \(de8a476375a5c940\).

For (10), the centered middle chord and first moments imply that the outer tangent midpoints are opposite. Denote the height-zero midpoint coordinate by \(c\); the outer endpoint coordinates are \(c\pm\ell_j/2\) and \(-c\pm\ell_j/2\). Put \(\kappa_i=(k_{ij}^++k_{ij}^-)/2\) for \(i=0,2\), and replace \(\tau\) by \(\tau'=\tau-\beta c\). Under the two additional middle hypotheses, its summand in (31) is zero. Expanding the outer summands gives
\[
\Delta_j(\tau')^2
+2\ell_j(\kappa_2-\kappa_0)\beta\tau'
+\frac{\ell_j^2\Delta_j}{4}\beta^2.
\]
Since \(\ell_j>0\), nonnegativity implies
\(|\kappa_2-\kappa_0|\le\Delta_j/2\); its two inequalities expand to (10).
At a tangent outer section, formula (26) remains valid, but the smooth endpoint graphs used in (28) are unavailable. No second differentiability or Hessian formula has been asserted in that case.

Finally, let \(S^\varepsilon\) be the smooth three-slice set constructed above. Its convex hull is compact, lies between heights zero and two, and by (14) has precisely these three integer-height sections. Its sections are smooth bodies rather than polygons, so this convex hull does not furnish the polytope required by a locked disproof. If the target bound were proved for every compatible smooth triple in the strict class (4), however, (3) would contradict the existence of any polygonal counterexample. This is the asserted reduction and its exact scope.
statement:
For a compatible triple of compact two-dimensional planar convex bodies, use the canonical notation
\[
S=\bigcup_{i=0}^2(\{i\}\times A_i),\qquad
a_i=|A_i|,\qquad T=a_0+a_1+a_2,\qquad t=\frac{2T}{9},
\]
and let \(\mu\) be the sum of planar area on these three slices. Write \(M=\max\{a_0,a_2\}\), \(m=\min\{a_0,a_2\}\), \(r=m/M\), and \(s=a_1/M\). Compatibility means \((A_0+A_2)/2\subseteq A_1\). Define \(h_S(y)=\inf_{H\ni y}\mu(H)\) and
\[
\mathcal D(A_0,A_1,A_2)
=\max_{y\in S}\inf_{H\ni y}\mu(H),
\tag{1}
\]
where \(H\) ranges over all closed halfspaces in \(\mathbb R^3\). The maximum in (1) exists, including for the nonpolytopal bodies used below.

Suppose \(A_0,A_1,A_2\) are polygons and constitute a counterexample to the locked problem. There exist compatible convex bodies \(A_i^\varepsilon\), for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\), whose boundaries are \(C^\infty\) regular simple closed curves with strictly positive curvature, such that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\max_i d_{\mathrm H}(A_i^\varepsilon,A_i)&\longrightarrow0,&
E_\varepsilon:=\sum_{i=0}^2|A_i^\varepsilon\mathbin{\triangle}A_i|
&\longrightarrow0,\\
\left|\mathcal D(A_0^\varepsilon,A_1^\varepsilon,A_2^\varepsilon)
       -\mathcal D(A_0,A_1,A_2)\right|&\le E_\varepsilon,&
|T^\varepsilon-T|&\le E_\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]
Here every superscripted area quantity is obtained from the superscripted bodies by the same definition. In particular,
\[
\mathcal D(A_0^\varepsilon,A_1^\varepsilon,A_2^\varepsilon)
<\frac{2T^\varepsilon}{9}.
\tag{3}
\]
The strict balanced and residual inequalities supplied for the original polygons by accepted facts \(15bb2c1680a0254e\) and \(291c24bb45bd4946\) persist:
\[
\begin{gathered}
a_i^\varepsilon<\frac{T^\varepsilon}{2}\quad(i=0,1,2),
\qquad 0<r^\varepsilon<\frac38,\\
\max\left\{1-r^\varepsilon,
 \frac{3r^\varepsilon+2\sqrt{r^\varepsilon}-1}{2}\right\}
<s^\varepsilon
<\min\{1+r^\varepsilon,\,2-r^\varepsilon\}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{4}
\]
More precisely, each of the finitely many positive differences in these strict inequalities can retain at least half its original value. The same assertion holds for any prescribed finite collection of strict continuous inequalities in the three positive areas.

For the remaining assertion, drop the superscript and let \(A_i\) denote any compatible \(C^\infty\) bodies with positive boundary curvature satisfying \(a_i<T/2\) and \(\mathcal D(A_0,A_1,A_2)<t\). Thus these \(A_i\) are auxiliary smooth bodies, not the original polygons. There are \(z\in\operatorname{int}A_1\), \(0<d<t\), three pairwise nonparallel unit vectors \(q_j\), real numbers \(\lambda_j\), and positive \(\alpha_j\), with
\[
\begin{aligned}
d&=\max_{w\in A_1}h_S((1,w)),&
\sum_{j=1}^3\alpha_j&=1,&
\sum_{j=1}^3\alpha_jq_j&=0,\\
\widehat H_j
&=\{(h,w):q_j\cdot(w-z)+\lambda_j(h-1)\le0\},&
\mu(\widehat H_j)&=d\quad(j=1,2,3).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]
Use exactly the cut normalization of accepted fact \(e4a8e2c026dd7346\). Define the full sections
\[
L_{ij}=A_i\cap\{w:q_j\cdot(w-z)+\lambda_j(i-1)=0\},
\qquad b_j=\mathcal H_1(L_{1j})>0.
\]
Empty sets and singleton sections have length and first moment zero. If \(c_{1j}\) is the midpoint of \(L_{1j}\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal H_1(L_{0j})&=\mathcal H_1(L_{2j})=:\ell_j\ge0,\\
\sum_{i=0}^2\int_{L_{ij}}(w-z)\,d\mathcal H_1(w)&=0,\\
0\le\ell_j&\le b_j,\qquad
\|z-c_{1j}\|
\le\frac{\ell_j(b_j-\ell_j)}{b_j+2\ell_j}
\le\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)b_j .
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
\]
If \(\ell_j=0\), both outer sections are empty or singletons, and \(c_{1j}=z\). If \(\ell_j>0\), both outer sections are full transverse chords; writing \(c_{ij}\) for their midpoints and \(c_j=(c_{0j}+c_{2j})/2\), one has
\[
\frac{L_{0j}+L_{2j}}2\subseteq L_{1j},
\qquad b_j(c_{1j}-z)+2\ell_j(c_j-z)=0.
\tag{7}
\]

For each \(j\) with \(\ell_j>0\), choose a unit vector \(p_j\perp q_j\) and coordinates \(\xi=q_j\cdot(w-z)\), \(\upsilon=p_j\cdot(w-z)\). At the endpoints of \(L_{ij}\), let \(\upsilon_{ij}^-<\upsilon_{ij}^+\), and let \(k_{ij}^\pm\) be the finite derivatives \(d\upsilon/d\xi\) of the actual smooth boundary at those endpoints. These are the smooth tangent-slope counterparts of the edge slopes in accepted fact \(de8a476375a5c940\), with exactly the same coordinate normalization. Set
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_j={}&(k_{0j}^+-k_{0j}^-)+(k_{2j}^+-k_{2j}^-),\\
\Gamma_j={}&(k_{2j}^+\upsilon_{2j}^+-k_{2j}^-\upsilon_{2j}^-)
 -(k_{0j}^+\upsilon_{0j}^+-k_{0j}^-\upsilon_{0j}^-),\\
\Theta_j={}&\sum_{i=0}^2
 \left[k_{ij}^+(\upsilon_{ij}^+)^2-k_{ij}^-(\upsilon_{ij}^-)^2\right].
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
Then
\[
\Delta_j\ge0,\qquad \Theta_j\ge0,\qquad
\Gamma_j^2\le\Delta_j\Theta_j.
\tag{9}
\]
No Hessian assertion at a tangent outer section is included in (9). If additionally \(\upsilon_{1j}^++\upsilon_{1j}^-=0\) and \(k_{1j}^+=k_{1j}^-\), then
\[
k_{0j}^+\ge k_{2j}^-,
\qquad k_{2j}^+\ge k_{0j}^-.
\tag{10}
\]
For smooth boundaries, the hypothesis \(k_{1j}^+=k_{1j}^-\) says that the derivative of the middle chord width vanishes at this cut; it does not assert that the width is constant on a neighborhood.

Only the strict area inequalities for the starting polygons are imported from the cited area facts. The depth normal form, attainment, smooth active family, first variations, and second variations are proved below for the auxiliary class; the polygon-only derivative conclusions of \(e4a8e2c026dd7346\) and \(de8a476375a5c940\) are not applied to smooth bodies. No convergence of chosen maximizing points or active cuts is required. An auxiliary smooth triple alone is not a disproof of the locked problem, which requires a polytope. Conversely, proving the target depth bound for all auxiliary smooth triples satisfying (4) would prove the locked polygonal theorem.
